system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2174-08-26 23:28:00 to 2174-08-28 17:05:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted with persistent epigastric pain and pain at the PICC site, following a recent hospitalization for gastritis treated with IV pantoprazole via PICC. Blood work was stable, ultrasound showed no DVT, and blood cultures were negative for infection. Given lack of symptom improvement on IV therapy, the PICC was removed and the patient was transitioned to oral pantoprazole. She tolerated a stage III bariatric diet and tube feeds, with improvement in symptoms. She was discharged home with oral medications and follow-up instructions. The hospital course was uncomplicated.
problems: Pain due to vascular prosthetic devices, implants and grafts, initial encounter
Surgical operation with implant of artificial internal device as the cause of abnormal reaction of the patient, or of later complication, without mention of misadventure at the time of the procedure

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I’ll be helping take care of you tonight. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, thanks. I woke up this morning with really bad burning pain in my upper belly—same spot as always. It’s constant and gets worse when I drink water.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any nausea or vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I threw up once today—just clear watery fluid. I haven’t been able to keep much down. I did pass gas and had a bowel movement this morning, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Any fever, chills, or chest pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no fever or anything like that. Just the pain and nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I see you were just discharged yesterday from bariatric surgery. What happened then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They said my ulcers weren’t healing well, so they started me on IV pantoprazole through a PICC line. But I didn’t feel any better, so they switched me back to pills and told me to stay NPO.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And now the pain is worse again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it came back full force this morning. I’ve tried my usual meds—acetaminophen, oral pantoprazole—but nothing helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ve reviewed your labs—everything looks stable. No signs of infection, liver issues, or pancreatitis. Your chest X-ray and belly X-ray are also clear—no blockage or free air.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing’s torn or blocked?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, both scans look normal. The bariatric surgery team was consulted and they don’t think you need surgery. We’ll manage this medically—focus on pain control and giving your gut a rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What’s the plan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you NPO for now, continue your tube feeds at goal rate, and give you IV fluids. We’ll also start IV pantoprazole to help reduce stomach acid. For pain, we’ll use IV morphine as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my G-tube is working okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it looks well-placed and we’ll keep using it for nutrition. We’ll also give you some medications by mouth to coat the stomach—like sucralfate and lidocaine viscous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but maybe a little less sharp. I haven’t vomited again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. Your labs this morning are still normal. We’re going to try advancing your diet slowly—start with clear liquids like water and broth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been scared to drink anything. What if it makes the pain worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll go slow. If you tolerate it, we’ll move to full liquids like cream of wheat or pudding. If it flares up, we’ll stop and stick with tube feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I can try that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well with the clear liquids. You had some cream of wheat and pudding without vomiting. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The pain is still there, but I didn’t feel sick after eating. That’s new.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think your pain might be due to a few things—reflux, slow stomach emptying, or bacterial overgrowth. We’re adding two new meds: erythromycin to help with motility and rifaximin to treat possible bacterial overgrowth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve heard of erythromycin as an antibiotic. Why are we using it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: At lower doses, it actually helps the stomach empty faster. It’s not for infection here. Rifaximin is a gut-targeted antibiotic that stays in the intestines and can help if there’s too much bacteria.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And what about H. pylori? Could that be causing this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked a blood test for H. pylori, but the results aren’t back yet. We’ll follow up on that at your next appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re thinking about discharge tomorrow. Your pain is more stable, you’re tolerating liquids, and your labs are fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. But will the pain go away?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might not go away completely right now. This is likely a long-term issue we’ll manage over time. The goal is to find a balance—meds, diet, and tube feeds—that lets you feel better and live well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’ll still need the G-tube at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue tube feeds at 50 mL/hr with Jevity 1.5. Your home formula will need to be updated—your outpatient team will help with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the new meds? How long do I take them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Erythromycin for 7 days, rifaximin for 7 days. But don’t stop them—discuss continuing at your follow-up with bariatric surgery. We’ve confirmed rifaximin is covered by your pharmacy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re going to discharge you this afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any restrictions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep doing tube feeds, drink water or Ensure shakes, and slowly add soft foods as tolerated. Avoid heavy meals. Take all your meds, including the new ones. Call if pain worsens or you can’t keep fluids down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See bariatric surgery soon. They’ll review the H. pylori result and decide next steps. We’ll send them a full summary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I’m nervous, but I feel like we have a plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You do. We’re here to support you. Take it one step at a time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check-in before discharge. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’ve got it. Keep using the tube, take the meds, go slow with food, and follow up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’re doing great. We’ll get your discharge papers ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One thing—should I be worried about the pain never going away?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It may not disappear completely, but we can manage it. It’ll take time and teamwork with your providers. The goal is improvement, not perfection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That helps. Thanks for being honest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. We’re in this together.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge orders are in. You’ll go home in the next few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I’m ready to be home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—you understand the meds, feeds, and follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Erythromycin and rifaximin for a week, pantoprazole, sucralfate, tube feeds at 50 mL/hr, and see bariatric surgery soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll call you in a few days to check in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I appreciate all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Let us know how you’re doing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Have a good day.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted with acute-on-chronic epigastric pain and nausea, shortly after a prior discharge from bariatric surgery. Labs and imaging were unremarkable, with no evidence of obstruction or infection. She was managed medically with NPO status, IV fluids, IV pantoprazole, and pain control. Tube feeds were continued, and she gradually advanced to clear and full liquids without emesis. New medications—erythromycin and rifaximin—were added to address possible bacterial overgrowth and dysmotility, and ranitidine was initiated for reflux. The patient’s pain stabilized, and she was discharged home with a plan to continue tube feeds, oral medications, and close follow-up with bariatric surgery to review H. pylori results and adjust treatment as needed.
